name: Thaalattu (Tharattu) — Kerala lullabies
tagline: Cradle songs sung by mothers and muthassis across Kerala
summary: Thaalattu (Tharattu) are Kerala's traditional lullabies — short melodic cradle songs sung by mothers and muthassis to soothe babies, teach values and pass local stories.
description: Thaalattu (also called tharattu, urakkupattu) are Kerala’s cradle songs: simple, repetitive melodies and rhymes that caregivers sing while rocking infants. Families sing them at home, in temples, and at cradle-ceremonies; muthassis (grandmothers) often keep the strongest repertory.

These songs matter because they carry language, local imagery and social memory. Lullabies range from everyday soothing refrains to composed classics such as Irayimman Thampi’s Omanathinkal Kidavo — a court lullaby from the early 19th century that remains widely known.

Today Kerala preserves and reuses these songs in many ways: popular film and devotional recordings, academic and community projects, and digital archives such as the First Songs initiative that records lullabies with same-language subtitles for learning and preservation.

A visitor to Kerala who listens for thaalattu finds living tradition: quiet home performances, recorded renditions in museums and concerts, short films and local festival events where lullaby themes appear in music and cinema.
highlights: Everyday oral tradition sung by mothers and muthassis
Recorded and archived in modern projects (First Songs)
Appears in Malayalam cinema, short films and cultural programmes
Used in public-health and community projects (e.g., Oorinte Tharattu)

sections.heading: Background
body: Lullabies in Kerala go by several names — tharattu, thaalattu, urakkupattu — and form part of a wider South Indian and pan‑Indian cradle‑song tradition. Some are anonymous folk refrains; others are court or literary compositions (for example Irayimman Thampi’s Omanathinkal Kidavo, composed for the Travancore royal household).

Researchers note that lullabies do more than induce sleep: they transmit vocabulary, local metaphors and social messages. Scholars and college projects in Kerala study their language, gender roles and cinematic uses.

sections.heading: Variations and where to hear them
body: Local variations reflect language, caste and religion; Christian, Hindu and Muslim households keep distinct repertories and devotional references. In performance, lullabies are short, often repetitive, and use imagery drawn from nature, domestic life and devotional sentiment.

Hear thaalattu in family homes, older neighbourhoods, cultural festivals, Kerala short‑film programmes and in recorded form on music platforms. Community archiving projects and the First Songs digital repository collect and show many examples with subtitles for wider access.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Listen: seek permission to listen to grandmothers and mothers sing at home; many families welcome visitors if introduced by a local contact. Visit cultural programmes, music festivals and short‑film screenings (lullaby themes appear in festival lineups).

Learn and sing: learn a simple verse from a caregiver and practise same‑language subtitled recordings (First Songs) to support basic Malayalam reading and to preserve the tune. Museums with sound archives or local cultural centres sometimes play historical recordings.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Plan village or home visits through a local guide or a cultural organisation; respect privacy and ask before recording or photographing infants. If you want recorded material, use community archives and digital collections rather than expecting family recordings on demand.

If your interest is academic or documentary, contact college departments, music schools or cultural bodies in Kochi and Thiruvananthapuram in advance — several local colleges and archives hold recordings and papers on lullaby traditions.

latest.text: Kerala’s state report (Kerala Report 2026) documents the Oorinte Tharattu neonatal‑care project in Attappady — a government programme that uses the lullaby metaphor in a public‑health initiative.
A viral video and local press coverage highlight grandmother (muthassi) lullabies in contemporary parenting and social media, showing how family thaalattu continue to circulate online.

The First Songs project (Bachpan Manao collaboration) publishes a pan‑India lullaby archive that includes Malayalam 'tharattu' videos with same‑language subtitles to support preservation and early literacy.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Any time of year — evening and night are best for hearing live lullabies; cultural festivals and film/music events add public performances.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Kerala is accessible via Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram or Kozhikode airports; travel by road and local buses to towns and villages. Use a local guide or cultural organisation to arrange home visits.
etiquette: Ask permission before recording or photographing a child or elder; many families prefer informal, verbal requests.
Bring a small gift or token of thanks when visiting a home; modest hospitality is common.
Learn one short verse to sing back — caregivers appreciate the effort and it helps build trust.
Use trusted digital archives (First Songs, local college collections) for recordings rather than requesting family archives on the spot.
